# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and rationale

Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has evolved through successive technological iterations, with randomized trials demonstrating progressive improvements in restenosis from balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents and subsequently to drug-eluting stents (DES) [1]. Despite the success of contemporary metallic DES, the permanent presence of a metal stent prevents coronary vasomotion, autoregulation, and adaptive coronary remodeling, and the limitations imposed by a permanent metal implant may be overcome with a bioresorbable scaffold [1]. The retained metallic frame and durable polymer can provoke persistent inflammation, neoatherosclerosis and late thrombotic events that continue to accrue beyond the first year [2]. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were conceived to provide transient mechanical support and drug delivery, followed by complete resorption and restoration of native vessel function [3].

## Early clinical development

The first-in-human evaluation of the everolimus-eluting poly-L-lactic acid Absorb scaffold (ABSORB Cohort A) established procedural feasibility [4], with later imaging and 2-year multimodality follow-up documenting bioresorption [5]. Four-year clinical outcomes of the ABSORB Cohort A trial demonstrated a low ischaemia-driven MACE rate of 3.4% without any scaffold thrombosis, with no additional events between six months and four years [6]. A second-generation device followed with improved imaging and clinical performance [7], and long-term invasive imaging suggested restoration of vasomotion, prevention of restenosis and increase in lumen area between six months and two years after Absorb BVS implantation [8].

## Pivotal randomized trials

The ABSORB II randomized trial compared the Absorb scaffold with the Xience everolimus-eluting metallic stent [9]. At 1 year, clinical and procedural secondary outcomes were broadly comparable [10], but at 3 years the trial did not meet its co-primary endpoints of superior vasomotor reactivity and non-inferior late luminal loss, and a higher rate of device-oriented composite endpoint due to target vessel myocardial infarction was observed in the Absorb group [11].

The pivotal ABSORB III trial, designed to support US approval [12], randomized 2008 patients [13]. Treatment of noncomplex obstructive coronary artery disease with the scaffold was within the prespecified margin for noninferiority with respect to target-lesion failure at 1 year [13]. However, between 1 and 3 years and cumulative to 3 years, adverse event rates—particularly target vessel myocardial infarction and scaffold thrombosis—were increased after BVS [14]. Five-year follow-up assessed outcomes beyond the point of complete resorption [15]. Patient-level pooled meta-analyses confirmed comparable 1-year outcomes [16] but excess events at 2 years across seven randomized trials [17].

## Safety concerns: scaffold thrombosis

The principal limitation that emerged was an elevated risk of scaffold thrombosis. A multicenter analysis characterized its clinical presentation, mechanisms and predictors [18], and registry data such as GHOST-EU reported concerning early event rates [18]. The investigator-initiated AIDA trial randomized patients in routine practice and was reported early on safety grounds; there was no significant difference in target-vessel failure, but the bioresorbable scaffold was associated with a significantly higher incidence of overall and very late device thrombosis than the metallic stent through 2 years [19]. A systematic review reported very late definite or probable scaffold thrombosis [20], and a dedicated meta-analysis found that BVS compared with EES was associated with higher risk for very late scaffold thrombosis between 1 and 2 years and scaffold thrombosis through 2 years [21]. At 3 years, BVS was associated with higher rates of target lesion failure and definite/probable scaffold thrombosis compared with DES [22], and a meta-analysis of 17 trials concluded BVS were inferior across safety and efficacy domains to 5 years, driven by elevated thrombosis [23].

## Mechanisms and procedural optimization

The higher event rates were attributed in part to device and technique factors. The higher scaffold thrombosis rates were likely due in part to bioresorbable polymers having insufficient radial strength, necessitating larger strut profiles [24]. Analyses from the ABSORB program demonstrated that operator technique—vessel size selection and pre- and post-dilation—influenced outcomes [25]. The ABSORB IV trial incorporated optimized implantation technique and broader patient selection [26], reporting non-inferior 30-day and 1-year rates of target lesion failure and angina compared with metallic DES, with a 1-year scaffold thrombosis rate of 0.7% [27]. Individual-patient pooled data indicated that excess risk concentrated within the first 3 years [28].

## Next-generation devices and current status

Attention has shifted to thinner-strut and metallic resorbable platforms. The magnesium-based Magmaris (DREAMS) scaffold was evaluated in BIOSOLVE-II, a first-in-man trial reporting acceptable late lumen loss at 6 months [29], and the device offers an alternative to polymeric scaffolds [29]. The final report of the ABSORB clinical program confirmed time-varying outcomes with excess target lesion failure and device thrombosis over 5 years [30]. The original Absorb device was withdrawn from the market, but iterative improvements in scaffold design and implantation technique continue to inform whether bioresorbable technology can ultimately fulfil its conceptual promise of vascular restoration without permanent implants [24].
